explainBack.prompt: Why does the government argue that copying newspaper articles to train an AI can be fair use, when copying an article to republish it clearly would not be?
explainBack.response: Because fair use is judged per use, not per act of copying. When articles are used in training, software adjusts numerical settings to extract statistical patterns of language; the purpose is building a tool that generates responses, not delivering those articles to readers. Republishing serves the same purpose as the original and substitutes for it, so the same copying gets a different legal question — just as recording a programme to watch later differs from selling the tape. And the filing itself concedes an output that reconstructs and distributes a work can raise yet another question.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: The stage separation and pattern-extraction mechanism (P005), the different-purpose argument (P006), the case-by-case factor framework (P007), and the VCR mapping with its retained limit (P008, P009).
explainBack.assessment: The article fully supports this answer: mechanism, purpose distinction, use-by-use framing and the output caveat are all present in the reader's ordinary language.

unseenTransfer.prompt: Using this article's mental model, is the vendor's conclusion sound?
unseenTransfer.response: No. The article's stage separation shows training legality and output legality are different questions. Even a lawfully trained model can produce an output that closely reconstructs an existing work, and publishing that output is a distinct use judged on its own — purpose, amount taken, market effect. The right move mirrors P011: before publishing any close-match output, ask what the basis is for using that specific passage, because a claim about training does not answer a question about your proposed use.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: The obtain/train/output pipeline (P005), the output-reconstruction caveat (P009), and the training-claim-doesn't-answer-use-question move (P011).
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism resolves this genuinely new scenario correctly and specifically, so transfer is demonstrated.

incidentExplained.observation: The September 1 filing, its nature, its arguments and its boundaries are explained in a followable causal sequence (P002, P003, P006).

artifactEvidence.excerpt: On September 1, the US Department of Justice submitted an argument supporting OpenAI in the New York copyright lawsuits. It urged the court to treat copying written work to teach AI patterns as fair use: certain uses US law permits without the copyright owner’s permission.

The document is a Statement of Interest—the government explaining its position to the court. It is not the court’s decision. What changed was the government’s intervention in the argument, not a new permission slip for everyone using AI.

The filing distinguishes the copyright questions at those stages. Its focus is copying works during training. The department argues that using articles to develop a tool that can generate responses has a different purpose from publishing those articles for people to read. It also argues that requiring developers to pay for permission to use works could make it harder for smaller AI developers to compete. These are reasons it gives the court for accepting its position.

The filing separates three things that can get bundled into “AI used someone’s work”. A developer first obtains material. During training, software adjusts numerical settings using examples, developing patterns it can apply later. The trained part that produces a response is the model. When someone uses it, the answer it produces is an output.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: Imagine AI gives you a paragraph very close to a newsletter you found online. This filing does not establish that you can put it in a client presentation. Ask the person responsible for the material, “What is our basis for using this passage?” A claim about the model’s training does not answer that question about your proposed use.

When the next headline says the copyright fight is settled, look for who actually decided what. A court ruling addressing a particular use would be a different development from this government filing. This report covers the September 1 submission; we have not verified a later ruling on its argument. And the discussion is about US law, not automatic permission in every country.
